cards.front: In what direction does the centripetal force act, and what effect does it have on the speed?
cards.back: Towards the centre of the circle, perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion but not the speed.

mcq.correct: Towards the centre of the circle, perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion but not the speed.
distractors: Outwards from the centre, increasing the speed
Along the direction of travel, keeping the speed constant
Towards the centre, increasing the speed

cards.explanation: A force at right angles to the motion does no work, so the kinetic energy and speed stay constant while the velocity keeps changing direction.

cards.front: Write the two expressions for centripetal acceleration.
cards.back: a = v^2/r and a = omega^2 r

mcq.correct: a = v^2/r and a = omega^2 r
distractors: a = v r^2 and a = omega r
a = v^2 r and a = omega/r
a = r/v^2 and a = r omega^2

cards.explanation: Substituting v = omega r into v^2/r turns one form into the other.

cards.front: Define angular velocity and give its unit.
cards.back: The rate of change of angle, omega = delta theta / delta t, in radians per second.

cards.front: A 900 kg car travels at 20 m/s round a bend of radius 50 m. Calculate the centripetal force needed.
cards.explanation: F = mv^2/r = 900 x 20^2 / 50 = 7200 N, supplied by friction between the tyres and the road.

cards.front: State the relationship between linear speed and angular velocity in circular motion.
cards.explanation: One full turn covers 2 pi r in a time T, and omega = 2 pi / T, so v = 2 pi r / T = omega r.

cards.front: A 0.50 kg mass on a 0.80 m string is whirled at 3.0 revolutions per second. Find the tension in the string.

keyPoints.text: convert revolutions per second to angular velocity

synonyms: use the angular form of the centripetal force

cards.explanation: $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 3.0 = 18.85\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, so $F = m\omega^2 r = 0.50 \times 355 \times 0.80 = 142\,\mathrm{N}$, or $140\,\mathrm{N}$ to two significant figures. Converting the frequency to radians per second is the step most often missed; using $f$ directly in place of $\omega$ gives an answer too small by a factor of $4\pi^2$.

cards.front: Find the minimum speed at which a car can pass over the top of a humpback bridge of radius 5.0 m without leaving the road.

keyPoints.text: at the minimum speed the normal contact force is zero
synonyms: the car is about to leave the road

keyPoints.text: the weight alone provides the centripetal force

cards.explanation: At the point of leaving the road the contact force vanishes, so $mg = \frac{mv^2}{r}$ and $v = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{9.81 \times 5.0} = 7.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The mass cancels, so the result is the same for a car and a lorry. Above this speed the required centripetal force exceeds the weight and the car leaves the surface - the same condition that governs the top of a loop-the-loop.

cards.front: State the relationship between period, frequency and angular velocity.
cards.back: $T = \frac{1}{f}$ and $\omega = 2\pi f = \frac{2\pi}{T}$, with $\omega$ in radians per second.

synonyms: period is the reciprocal of frequency
angular velocity is 2 pi times the frequency

cards.explanation: The factor $2\pi$ converts revolutions to radians, since one revolution is $2\pi$ radians. Omitting it is the standard error and gives an angular velocity too small by about 6.3. Angular velocity is measured in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ while frequency is in hertz, and the two are numerically equal only when angles are counted in revolutions.

cards.front: Is centripetal force a new kind of force? Explain what it is.
cards.back: No. It is the name given to the resultant force towards the centre, whatever supplies it - tension, friction, gravity or a normal contact force.

keyPoints.text: it is not a separate force
synonyms: not a new type of force
it is a role, not a source

keyPoints.text: it is the resultant force towards the centre

mcq.correct: No; it is the resultant inward force, supplied by tension, friction or gravity
distractors: Yes; it is a fifth fundamental force
Yes; it acts outwards on a rotating body
No; it is another name for the weight

cards.explanation: On a free-body diagram you never draw a force labelled 'centripetal'; you draw the real forces and identify their inward resultant. For a car on a flat bend it is friction between tyre and road, for a satellite it is gravity, and for a mass on a string it is tension. The outward 'centrifugal force' appears only in a rotating frame of reference and is not a real force.

cards.front: A conical pendulum has a bob moving in a horizontal circle. Explain which forces provide the centripetal force.
cards.back: The weight acts downwards and the tension acts along the string. The horizontal component of the tension provides the centripetal force, while its vertical component balances the weight.

keyPoints.text: the tension acts along the string
synonyms: at an angle to the vertical

keyPoints.text: the horizontal component of the tension is the centripetal force
the vertical component balances the weight

mcq.correct: Horizontal component of tension inward; vertical component balances the weight
distractors: The tension alone, acting along the string
The weight provides the centripetal force
An outward centrifugal force balances the tension

cards.explanation: Resolving gives $T\cos\theta = mg$ vertically and $T\sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r}$ horizontally, and dividing one by the other gives $\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{gr}$, which is why a faster bob swings out further. Note that the tension is not itself the centripetal force, because it is not horizontal - only its component is.

cards.front: Estimate the centripetal acceleration of a person standing on the equator, taking the Earth's radius as $6.4 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$.
cards.explanation: $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{86400} = 7.27 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, so $a = \omega^2 r = 0.034\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, which is under 0.4% of $g$. That smallness is why the Earth's rotation is rarely noticed in everyday mechanics, though it is measurable: $g$ at the equator is slightly less than at the poles for this reason as well as because of the Earth's bulge.

cards.front: A 900 kg car rounds a flat bend of radius 60 m. The maximum friction force available is 6000 N. Find the maximum speed.

synonyms: the maximum friction sets the limit

keyPoints.text: F = mv^2 / r so v = sqrt(Fr/m)

cards.explanation: $v = \sqrt{\frac{Fr}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{6000 \times 60}{900}} = \sqrt{400} = 20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Above this speed the required centripetal force exceeds what friction can supply and the car skids outwards along a tangent, not radially. This is why a wet or icy road, which lowers the friction, lowers the safe speed for the same bend.
